newsitem.title: GERMANY: Werner leaves Daimler nice 1996 Mercedes profit.
newsitem.headline: Werner leaves Daimler nice 1996 Mercedes profit.

text.p: Former Mercedes boss Helmut Werner unceremoniously left Daimler-Benz AG in January after losing a nasty power fight with Juergen Schrempp but left his former boss a gift of higher 1996 profits at Daimler's carmaker unit.

Daimler, which merged Mercedes into its group structure in April from its status as a separate unit, said on Wednesday operating profit at Mercedes rose 27 percent to 2.71 billion marks from 1995 and was again Daimler's dominant profit centre.
The Stuttgart-based industrial group earlier this year reported a 10 percent gain in operating profit for 1996 and a 10 percent rise in sales to 106.3 billion marks.
Schrempp is not yet done receiving nice gifts from Werner, who lost the unusually public powerplay in late 1995 for control of Germany's largest industrial group.

Mercedes will launch in May its new A-class compact, a car at the centre of Werner's aim to widen Mercedes's product offering into smaller and sportier cars while still keeping up the Stuttgart-based carmaker's tradition for luxury vehicles.

Werner had a relatively free hand at Mercedes under former Daimler chief Edzard Reuter and took a strong interest in the development of the car, which has received positive reviews in the motor press since its March debut at the Geneva car show.

Schrempp, named chief executive in 1995, was rumoured to have reservations about Mercedes' foray into the small car vehicle market, which also includes a joint venture with Swiss watchmaker Swatch to build a microcar, and face aggressive competition from lower-cost vehicle producers.

But Daimler management board member Dieter Zetsche told the group's annual news conference on Wednesday that Mercedes now has some 330,000 names of potential customers for the A-class and what he called some 100,000 "very hot" potential customers.

Mercedes executives have also said they were comfortable with a first-year sales goal of 200,000 A-class vehicles, helping along what industry analysts have said was Mercedes' ability to implement a strong organic growth policy.

But Schrempp will soon face a stiff test since Daimler said on Wednesday demand for passenger cars was inconsistent in the 1997 first quarter when car sales rose 1.1 percent to 11.4 billion marks and unit sales rose four percent to 154,011 but output slowed one percent to 161,696 units.

Despite a 26 percent rise in U.S. sales, Daimler said demand for new car sales in Germany declined along with the market in the first quarter. Many European markets -- France, Holland, Switzerland and Austria -- were all below year-ago levels.

Mercedes' commercial vehicle unit, which eroded the passenger car unit's 1996 operating profit of 3.1 billion marks by 400 million marks, also noted an "extremely difficult market situation" in western Europe and in North America.

Daimler management board member Kurt Lauck, who oversees the commercial truck unit, said first quarter sales were up 10 percent to 8.16 billion marks but that limited availablity of the new Actros heavy truck hampered sales efforts along with recessionary construction industry conditions around the world.
Despite the cautious outlook at Mercedes, Schrempp said the automotive business would develop "significantly more favourably" than the rest of the industry.
Schrempp still has his work cut out in other areas of Daimler after he predicted all five divisions would post an operating profit in 1997.

Daimler-Benz Aerospace AG (Dasa) unit, where Schrempp spent most of his career, reported a 1996 loss of 196 million marks after a staggering 7.2 billion mark loss in 1995 as he set about restructuring Daimler and dumping Dutch aircraft maker Fokker.
Only Daimler's Debis information services unit also reported an operating profit for 1996 among Daimler's five major units, rising to 288 million marks from 112 million marks in 1995.
